sword_marker_records.content_osis: <div sID="gen13195" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="143" osisID="Ps.143" sID="Ps.143"/> <div eID="gen13195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13196" type="x-p"/> This psalm, as those before, is a prayer of David, and full of complaints of the great distress and danger he was in, probably when Saul persecuted him. He did not only pray in that affliction, but he prayed very much and very often, not the same over again, but new thoughts. In this psalm, I. He complains of his troubles, through the oppression of his enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.3">ver. 3</reference>) and the weakness of his spirit under it, which was ready to sink notwithstanding the likely course he took to support himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.4-Ps.143.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. II. He prays, and prays earnestly (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.6">ver. 6</reference>), 1. That God would hear him, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1-Ps.143.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. 2. That he would not deal with him according to his sins, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.2">ver. 2</reference>. 3. That he would not hide his face from him (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.7">ver. 7</reference>), but manifest his favour to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.8">ver. 8</reference>. 4. That he would guide and direct him in the way of his duty (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.8">ver. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.10">10</reference>) and quicken him in it, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.11">ver. 11</reference>. 5. That he would deliver him out of his troubles, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.9">ver. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.11">11</reference>. 6. That he would in due time reckon with his persecutors, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.12">ver. 12</reference>. We may more easily accommodate this psalm to ourselves, in the singing of it, because most of the petitions in it are for spiritual blessings (which we all need at all times), mercy and grace.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen13196" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Complaints and Petitions.</title> <div sID="gen13197" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear my prayer, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , give ear to my supplications: in thy faithfulness answer me, <hi type="italic">and</hi> in thy righteousness. <hi type="super">2</hi> And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified. <hi type="super">3</hi> For the enemy hath persecuted my soul; he hath smitten my life down to the ground; he hath made me to dwell in darkness, as those that have been long dead. <hi type="super">4</hi> Therefore is my spirit overwhelmed within me; my heart within me is desolate. <hi type="super">5</hi> I remember the days of old; I meditate on all thy works; I muse on the work of thy hands. <hi type="super">6</hi> I stretch forth my hands unto thee: my soul <hi type="italic">thirsteth</hi> after thee, as a thirsty land. Selah. <div eID="gen13197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13198" type="x-p"/> Here, I. David humbly begs to be heard (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.1">v. 1</reference>), not as if he questioned it, but he earnestly desired it, and was in care about it, for, having desired it, and was in care about it, for having directed his prayer, he looked up to see how it sped, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Hab. ii. 1</reference>. He is a suppliant to his God, and he begs that his requests may be granted: <hi type="italic">Hear my prayer; give ear to my supplications.</hi> He is an appellant against his persecutors, and he begs that his case may be brought to hearing and that God will give judgment upon it, in his faithfulness and righteousness, as the Judge of right and wrong. Or, "Answer my petitions in thy faithfulness, according to the promises thou hast made, which thou wilt be just to." We have no righteousness of our own to plead, and therefore must plead God's righteousness, the word of promise which he has freely given us and caused us to hope in. <div eID="gen13198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13199" type="x-p"/> II. He humbly begs not to be proceeded against in strict justice, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.2">v. 2</reference>. He seems here, if not to correct, yet to explain, his plea (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.1">v. 1</reference>), Deliver me <hi type="italic">in thy righteousness;</hi> "I mean," says he, "the righteous promises of the gospel, not the righteous threatenings of the law; if I be answered according to the righteousness of this broken covenant of innocency, I am quite undone;" and therefore, 1. His petition is, "<hi type="italic">Enter not into judgment with thy servant;</hi> do not deal with me in strict justice, as I deserve to be dealt with." In this prayer we must own ourselves to be God's servants, bound to obey him, accountable to him, and solicitous to obtain his favour, and we must approve ourselves to him. We must acknowledge that in many instances we have offended him, and have come short of our duty to him, that he might justly enquire into our offences, and proceed against us for them according to law, and that, if he should do so, judgment would certainly go against us; we have nothing to move in arrest or mitigation of it, but execution would be taken out and awarded and then we should be ruined for ever. But we must encourage ourselves with a hope that there is mercy and forgiveness with God, and be earnest with him for the benefit of that mercy. "<hi type="italic">Enter not into judgment with thy servant,</hi> for thou hast already entered into judgment with thy Son, and laid upon him the iniquity of us all. <hi type="italic">Enter not into judgment with thy servant,</hi> for thy servant enters into judgment with himself;" and, if <hi type="italic">we will judge ourselves, we shall not be judged.</hi> 2. His plea is, "<hi type="italic">In thy sight shall no man living be justified</hi> upon those terms, for no man can plead innocency nor any righteousness of his own, either that he has not sinned or that he does not deserve to die for his sins; nor that he has any satisfaction of his own to offer;" nay, if God contend with us, <hi type="italic">we are not able to answer him for one of a thousand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.9.3">Job ix. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.20">xv. 20</reference>. David, before he prays for the removal of his trouble, prays for the pardon of his sin, and depends upon mere mercy for it. <div eID="gen13199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13200" type="x-p"/> III. He complains of the prevalency of his enemies against him (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.3">v. 3</reference>): "Saul, that great enemy, <hi type="italic">has persecuted my soul,</hi> sought my life, with a restless malice, and has carried the persecution so far that he has already <hi type="italic">smitten it down to the ground.</hi> Though I am not yet under ground, I am struck to the ground, and that is next door to it; he has forced me to <hi type="italic">dwell in darkness,</hi> not only in dark caves, but in dark thoughts and apprehensions, in the clouds of melancholy, <hi type="italic">as</hi> helpless and hopeless as <hi type="italic">those that have been long dead.</hi> Lord, let me find mercy with thee, for I find no mercy with men. They condemn me; but, Lord, do not thou condemn me. Am not I an object of thy compassion, fit to be appeared for; and is not my enemy an object of thy displeasure, fit to be appeared against?" <div eID="gen13200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13201" type="x-p"/> IV. He bemoans the oppression of his mind, occasioned by his outward troubles (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore is my spirit</hi> overpowered and <hi type="italic">overwhelmed within me,</hi> and I am almost plunged in despair; when without are fightings within are fears, and those fears greater tyrants and oppressors than Saul himself and not so easily out-run. It is sometimes the lot of the best men to have their spirits for a time almost overwhelmed and their hearts desolate, and doubtless it is their infirmity. David was not only a great saint, but a great soldier, and yet even he was sometimes ready to faint in a day of adversity. <hi type="italic">Howl, fir-trees, if the cedars be shaken.</hi> <div eID="gen13201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13202" type="x-p"/> V. He applies himself to the use of proper means for the relief of his troubled spirit. He had no force to muster up against the oppression of the enemy, but, if he can keep possession of nothing else, he will do what he can to keep possession of his own soul and to preserve his inward peace. In order to this, 1. He looks back, and <hi type="italic">remembers the days of old</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.5">v. 5</reference>), God's former appearances for his afflicted people and for him in particular. It has been often a relief to the people of God in their straits to think of the wonders which their fathers told them of, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.5">Ps. lxxvii. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.11">11</reference>. 2. He looks round, and takes notice of the works of God in the visible creation, and the providential government of the world: <hi type="italic">I meditate on all thy works.</hi> Many see them, but do not see the footsteps of God's wisdom, power, and goodness in them, and do not receive the benefit they might by them because they do not meditate upon them; they do not dwell on that copious curious subject, but soon quit it, as if they had exhausted it, when they have scarcely touched upon it. <hi type="italic">I muse on,</hi> or (as some read it) <hi type="italic">I discourse of, the</hi> operation <hi type="italic">of thy hands,</hi> how great, how good, it is! The more we consider the power of God the less we shall fear the face or force of man, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12-Isa.51.13">Isa. li. 12, 13</reference>. 3. He looks up with earnest desires towards God and his favour (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I stretch forth my hands unto thee,</hi> as one begging an alms, and big with expectation to receive something great, standing ready to lay hold on it and bid it welcome. <hi type="italic">My soul thirsteth after thee; it is to thee</hi> (so the word is), entire for thee, intent on thee; it is <hi type="italic">as a thirsty land,</hi> which, being parched with excessive heat, gapes for rain; so do I need, so do I crave, the support and refreshment of divine consolations under my afflictions, and nothing else will relieve me." This is the best course we can take when our spirits are overwhelmed; and justly do those sink under their load who will not take such a ready way as this to ease themselves.

David was not only a great saint, but a great soldier, and yet even he was sometimes ready to faint in a day of adversity. <hi type="italic">Howl, fir-trees, if the cedars be shaken.</hi> <div eID="gen13201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13202" type="x-p"/> V. He applies himself to the use of proper means for the relief of his troubled spirit. He had no force to muster up against the oppression of the enemy, but, if he can keep possession of nothing else, he will do what he can to keep possession of his own soul and to preserve his inward peace. In order to this, 1. He looks back, and <hi type="italic">remembers the days of old</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.5">v. 5</reference>), God's former appearances for his afflicted people and for him in particular. It has been often a relief to the people of God in their straits to think of the wonders which their fathers told them of, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.5">Ps. lxxvii. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.11">11</reference>. 2. He looks round, and takes notice of the works of God in the visible creation, and the providential government of the world: <hi type="italic">I meditate on all thy works.</hi> Many see them, but do not see the footsteps of God's wisdom, power, and goodness in them, and do not receive the benefit they might by them because they do not meditate upon them; they do not dwell on that copious curious subject, but soon quit it, as if they had exhausted it, when they have scarcely touched upon it. <hi type="italic">I muse on,</hi> or (as some read it) <hi type="italic">I discourse of, the</hi> operation <hi type="italic">of thy hands,</hi> how great, how good, it is! The more we consider the power of God the less we shall fear the face or force of man, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12-Isa.51.13">Isa. li. 12, 13</reference>. 3. He looks up with earnest desires towards God and his favour (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I stretch forth my hands unto thee,</hi> as one begging an alms, and big with expectation to receive something great, standing ready to lay hold on it and bid it welcome. <hi type="italic">My soul thirsteth after thee; it is to thee</hi> (so the word is), entire for thee, intent on thee; it is <hi type="italic">as a thirsty land,</hi> which, being parched with excessive heat, gapes for rain; so do I need, so do I crave, the support and refreshment of divine consolations under my afflictions, and nothing else will relieve me." This is the best course we can take when our spirits are overwhelmed; and justly do those sink under their load who will not take such a ready way as this to ease themselves.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen13202" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayers for Divine Grace.</title> <div sID="gen13203" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Hear me speedily, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> : my spirit faileth: hide not thy face from me, lest I be like unto them that go down into the pit. <hi type="super">8</hi> Cause me to hear thy lovingkindness in the morning; for in thee do I trust: cause me to know the way wherein I should walk; for I lift up my soul unto thee. <hi type="super">9</hi> Deliver me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , from mine enemies: I flee unto thee to hide me. <hi type="super">10</hi> Teach me to do thy will; for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my God: thy spirit <hi type="italic">is</hi> good; lead me into the land of uprightness. <hi type="super">11</hi> Quicken me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , for thy name's sake: for thy righteousness' sake bring my soul out of trouble. 12 And of thy mercy cut off mine enemies, and destroy all them that afflict my soul: for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> thy servant. <div eID="gen13203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13204" type="x-p"/> David here tells us what he said when he stretched forth his hands unto God; he begins not only as one in earnest, but as one in haste: "<hi type="italic">Hear me speedily,</hi> and defer no longer, for <hi type="italic">my spirit faileth.</hi> I am just ready to faint; reach the cordial—quickly, quickly, or I am gone." It was not a haste of unbelief, but of vehement desire and holy love. <hi type="italic">Make haste, O God! to help me.</hi> Three things David here prays for:— <div eID="gen13204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13205" type="x-p"/> I. The manifestations of God's favour towards him, that God would be well pleased with him and let him know that he was so; this he prefers before any good, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Ps. iv. 6</reference>. 1. He dreads God's frowns: "Lord, <hi type="italic">hide not thy face from me;</hi> Lord, be not angry with me, do not turn from me, as we do from one we are displeased with; Lord, let me not be left under the apprehensions of thy anger or in doubt concerning thy favour; if I have thy favour, let it not be hidden from me." Those that have the truth of grace cannot but desire the evidence of it. He pleads the wretchedness of his case if God withdrew from him: "Lord, let me not lie under thy wrath, for then I am <hi type="italic">like those that go down to the pit,</hi> that is, down to the grave (I am a dead man, weak, and pale, and ghastly; thy frowns are worse than death), or down to hell, the bottomless pit." Even those who through grace are delivered from going down to the pit may sometimes, when the terrors of the Almighty set themselves in array against them, look like those who are going to the pit. Disconsolate saints have sometimes cried out of the wrath of God, as if they had been damned sinners, <reference osisRef="Job.6.4">Job vi. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.6">Ps. lxxxviii. 6</reference>. 2. He entreats God's favour (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Cause me to hear thy lovingkindness in the morning.</hi> He cannot but think that God has a kindness for him, that he has some kind things to say to him, some good words and comfortable words; but the present hurry of his affairs, and tumult of his spirits, drowned those pleasing whispers; and therefore he begs, "Lord, do not only speak kindly to me, but cause me to hear it, to <hi type="italic">hear joy and gladness,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.51.8">Ps. li. 8</reference>. God's goodness is commonly wrought <hi type="italic">for those who trust in him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.8">Ps. xxxi. 8</reference>), who by faith draw it out. <div eID="gen13205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13206" type="x-p"/> II. The operations of God's grace in him. Those he is as earnest for as for the tokens of God's favour to him, and so should we be. He prays, <div eID="gen13206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13207" type="x-p"/> 1. That he might be enlightened with the knowledge of God's will; and this is the first work of the Spirit, in order to his other works, for God deals with men as men, as reasonable creatures. Whatever trouble I am in, Lord, let not my heart be troubled," <reference osisRef="John.14.1">John xiv. 1</reference>. 2. That he would reckon with those that were the instruments of his trouble (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Of thy mercy</hi> to me <hi type="italic">cut off my enemies,</hi> that I may be no longer in fear of them; <hi type="italic">and destroy all those,</hi> whoever they be, how numerous, how powerful, soever, <hi type="italic">who afflict my soul,</hi> and create vexation to that; <hi type="italic">for I am thy servant,</hi> and am resolved to continue such, and therefore may expect to be owned and protected in thy service." This prayer is a prophecy of the utter destruction of all the impenitent enemies of Jesus Christ and his kingdom, who will not have him to reign over them, who grieve his Spirit, and afflict his soul, by afflicting his people, in whose afflictions he is afflicted.  <chapter eID="Ps.143"/> <div eID="gen13209" type="x-p"/>

navigation_sections.content_plain: This psalm, as those before, is a prayer of David, and full of complaints of the great distress and danger he was in, probably when Saul persecuted him. He did not only pray in that affliction, but he prayed very much and very often, not the same over again, but new thoughts. In this psalm, I. He complains of his troubles, through the oppression of his enemies ( ver. 3 ) and the weakness of his spirit under it, which was ready to sink notwithstanding the likely course he took to support himself, ver. 4, 5 . II. He prays, and prays earnestly ( ver. 6 ), 1. That God would hear him, ver. 1-7 . 2. That he would not deal with him according to his sins, ver. 2 . 3. That he would not hide his face from him ( ver. 7 ), but manifest his favour to him, ver. 8 . 4. That he would guide and direct him in the way of his duty ( ver. 8 , 10 ) and quicken him in it, ver. 11 . 5. That he would deliver him out of his troubles, ver. 9 , 11 . 6. That he would in due time reckon with his persecutors, ver. 12 . We may more easily accommodate this psalm to ourselves, in the singing of it, because most of the petitions in it are for spiritual blessings (which we all need at all times), mercy and grace.
navigation_sections.content_osis: <div sID="gen13195" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="143" osisID="Ps.143" sID="Ps.143"/> <div eID="gen13195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13196" type="x-p"/> This psalm, as those before, is a prayer of David, and full of complaints of the great distress and danger he was in, probably when Saul persecuted him. He did not only pray in that affliction, but he prayed very much and very often, not the same over again, but new thoughts. In this psalm, I. He complains of his troubles, through the oppression of his enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.3">ver. 3</reference>) and the weakness of his spirit under it, which was ready to sink notwithstanding the likely course he took to support himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.4-Ps.143.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. II. He prays, and prays earnestly (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.6">ver. 6</reference>), 1. That God would hear him, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1-Ps.143.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. 2. That he would not deal with him according to his sins, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.2">ver. 2</reference>. 3. That he would not hide his face from him (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.7">ver. 7</reference>), but manifest his favour to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.8">ver. 8</reference>. 4. That he would guide and direct him in the way of his duty (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.8">ver. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.10">10</reference>) and quicken him in it, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.11">ver. 11</reference>. 5. That he would deliver him out of his troubles, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.9">ver. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.11">11</reference>. 6. That he would in due time reckon with his persecutors, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.12">ver. 12</reference>. We may more easily accommodate this psalm to ourselves, in the singing of it, because most of the petitions in it are for spiritual blessings (which we all need at all times), mercy and grace.
